newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Ibrahim stands up to foreign airlines.
newsitem.headline: India's Ibrahim stands up to foreign airlines.

text.p: Indian Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim has reiterated his strong opposition to foreign airlines holding equity stakes in domestic operators, but added he was not ruling out stakes for them in future.
In an interview published in the Business Standard newspaper on Friday, Ibrahim said he expected Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways to sell off their stakes in private carrier Jet Airways.
Last week the government agreed to allow foreign investors to take stakes of up to 40 percent in private domestic airlines.
But under strong pressure from Ibrahim and state-owned Indian Airlines, the cabinet barred foreign airlines from investing in domestic carriers pending a review by the Civil Aviation Ministry.
"We have no objection to 40 percent equity holding by foreign investors," Ibrahim said. "But no foreign airline directly or indirectly should be allowed to have any say in the domestic set-up."
Ibrahim said the cabinet had told his ministry to re-examine the possibility of allowing foreign carriers to take equity stakes in domestic airlines.
Singapore Airlines Ltd has proposed setting up a $600 million joint airline venture with India's Tata group. But last week's cabinet decision put a hold on the proposed project.

"In future, I can't say I may not allow foreign airlines," Ibrahim said. "But now at present, this is the situation....Anyone from Singapore can come and invest. Except for airlines, anyone can enter the domestic aviation sector."

Asked if India could stop Singapore Airlines from investing in a venture with the Tatas through "a front company", Ibrahim said the government would have to look at the company's capital structure and related matters.
"Will Singapore allow Indian Airlines to buy shares in Singapore domestic airlines?" he said. "They don't allow more than five percent shares to anyone."

The cabinet minister said he expected Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways to sell off their stakes in Jet Airways, one of a handful of private domestic carriers which sprung up after India began opening its airline sector in 1994.
Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways each hold 20 percent stakes in Jet, worth $4 million each.

"Now the existing policy has already allowed 40 percent equity holding to Jet Airways," Ibrahim said. "They have to come forward and shed that voluntarily. Otherwise a wrong signal will go out that we are supporting a particular company."

Ibrahim was asked when the government would ask Jet Airways to do so. "I think Jet Airways will understand and may do it voluntarily. But from our side, we will start formal initiatives," he said without elaborating.
A Jet Airways official told Reuters on Friday: "If we are asked to disinvest, we will do it."
